text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Over half of the car drivers that are aged 65 and over and involved in a traffic accident have signs of early senile dementia, according to a study from Huddinge Hospital.

- Nordbanken economists expected the economy to see better times after a weak 1997. From 1998 to 2000 the bank forecasts Gross Domestic Product to grow by over three percent a year but the economists forecast for 1997 was more pessimistic now than it was in February.
- A new investigation finds the Swedish government knew that gold given to Sweden by the Nazis had been stolen from Jews. The information was released on television programme Actuellt.

- The Gothenburg Post said internal documents in vehicle maker Volvo showed the company expected to earn six billion crowns this year. In the longer term Volvo was aiming for an operating profit of 10 billion crowns. Dividends would rise by 10 percent if everything went to plan, according to the internal memo.

- Sweden will enter its strongest economic growth phase in three decades with gross domestic product (GDP) rising 3.5 percent in 1998, 3.8 percent in 1999 and 3.3 percent in 2000, compared to 1.1 percent in 1996, bank Nordbanken forecast. However unemployment will remain at a high level for Sweden at 7.4 percent in 1998, 6.5 percent in 1999 and 5.5 percent in 2000, compared to March levels of 8.4 percent.

- The World Wildlife Fund (WWF) received a gift of nearly four million crowns from engineer ABB last autumn, at the time of an environmental debate about ABB building the Bakun dam in Malaysia. WWF has critisised the Bakun dam less than other environmental associations.

- Mining companies prospecting for gold and exploiting deposits can find it tougher if the "gold deposit of the century" in Busang, Indonesia, proves to be a flop where investors were mislead by false information.

- Parallel imports of Astra's anti-ulcer drug Losec from Italy are taking market share from Losec made in Sweden -- maybe as much as 20-25 percent. Cross Pharma in southern Sweden buys Losec made under licence in Italy and imports it to Sweden. It is then repackaged with Swedish information. Italian Losec is about 15 percent cheaper.

- The Stockholm Borsinformation (SBI) has become something of a greenhouse for high-tech start-up companies in Sweden who can list their shares before they are ready for the stricter demands and costs of the Stockholm Stockholm Exchange (SSE). The SBI was started by Henrik Andersson to give fledgling corporations a head start.

- Stronger economic growth and higher inflation await Swedes in 1998, according to a report from Nordbanken. The bank forecasts growth of 1.7 percent in 1997 and 3.5 percent from 1998 to 2000. Nordbanken economists cite a robust export sector and accelerating private consumption as the basis for the bright outlook.

- The Gothenburg Post newspaper reported that Volvo expects to make an operating profit of six billion crowns this year, according to internal budget estimates acquired by the paper. The internal memo puts Volvo Cars' profit for January-February this year at 375 million crowns on sales four percent better than expected. The dividend for 1997 should be about 10 percent higher than 1996.
